strengths: JoVA proposes a simple unified transformer architecture for joint video-audio generation, using joint self-attention over concatenated video, audio, and text tokens instead of explicit cross-attention/fusion modules. This design is clean and preserves pretrained modality knowledge while enabling direct cross-modal interaction.

The mouth-area loss is simple to implement and is shown to substantially improve lip-sync accuracy, with LSE-C increasing from 1.39 at λ=0 to 6.64 at λ=5.0 on UniAvatar-Bench. The appendix zero-masking validation provides useful evidence that the latent-space mouth masks are reasonably well localized.

The paper presents extensive quantitative comparisons on UniAvatar-Bench and Verse-Bench across lip-sync, TTS, audio quality, and video quality metrics. It also compares against both audio-driven and unified video-audio baselines, and demonstrates efficient small-model performance with a 3.2B variant.

The training data construction pipeline is broad, covering text2audio, text2video-audio, and text2avatar-speech data with multi-level captions and ASR transcripts. This is a useful engineering contribution for multimodal speech-video generation.
Ablations on mouth-loss weight, temporal-aligned RoPE, and joint self-attention versus cross-attention variants support the main architectural and training choices.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: joint self-attention over concatenated multimodal tokens is a standard multimodal transformer design, and the mouth-area loss is essentially a reweighted/masked flow-matching loss. The work is mostly an effective engineering combination rather than a fundamentally new method.

Reproducibility details are insufficient for a 12B/24B-scale model. The paper does not specify how audio and video latent dimensions are projected into the shared attention dimension, which facial keypoint detector is used, inference resolution/duration/steps, optimizer details, hardware, or whether code/models/data will be released. These omissions are significant for an ECCV paper.

The SOTA claim is not fully supported. On Verse-Bench, OVI outperforms JoVA on LSE-C, FD, CU, PC, and PQ, so the advantage is mixed. On UniAvatar-Bench, JoVA is evaluated on a benchmark introduced by the authors, with only 100 samples and limited construction details, no variance/error bars, and no human evaluation.

The paper contains clarity and consistency issues. For example, the text says JoVA’s LSE-C of 6.51 “slightly underperforms OVI (6.41)” while the table reports OVI at 6.61; the benchmark is called both Universe-Bench and Verse-Bench; and the cross-attention with linear adaptation result (LSE-C 1.63) is anomalously poor and not explained.

The mouth-aware supervision may not generalize to the broad video-audio scenarios claimed. It relies on reliable facial keypoint detection and visible mouth regions; handling of missing faces, small faces, profile views, occlusion, multiple speakers, non-human videos, and ambient-sound-only clips is not discussed.

The 700-hour talking-head data collection from public sources raises privacy, consent, and licensing questions that are not adequately addressed beyond a brief declaration. The evaluation lacks discussion of identity overlap, data contamination, or demographic diversity of speech/face data.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: joint video-audio generation with human speech and lip synchronization, which is central to human-centric multimodal generation.

The core architecture is conceptually simple: concatenating video, audio, and text tokens and applying joint self-attention within each transformer block. This avoids explicit cross-attention/fusion modules and leverages pretrained Waver/MMAudio backbones, making the design easy to describe and potentially extensible.

The mouth-area loss is simple and the ablation in Table 3 shows a large improvement in lip-sync accuracy (LSE-C from 1.39 to 6.64) when the mouth loss is used, without obvious degradation in the reported audio/video quality metrics.

The evaluation uses a broad set of metrics (LSE-C, WER, FD/KL, CLAP, AudioBox-Aesthetics, motion, aesthetic, identity consistency) and includes comparisons on two benchmarks as well as a smaller 3.2B-parameter variant, which helps assess scalability.

The training-data construction pipeline with video captions, audio captions, and Whisper transcripts is a reasonable attempt to provide multi-level supervision for speech-aware video-audio generation.
Qualitative examples in Figure 5 support the claim that the model can produce intelligible speech with plausible lip-sync in selected cases.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. Joint self-attention over concatenated multimodal tokens is a standard design in multimodal transformers (e.g., MM-DiT-style architectures); this paper largely applies that pattern to video-audio-text. The mouth-area loss is a straightforward weighted flow-matching loss on detected mouth boxes, not a new learning principle or architecture.

The paper claims to avoid additional alignment modules, but it explicitly adopts temporal-aligned RoPE, which is an alignment mechanism, and still uses separate video/audio VAEs and modality-specific branches/parameters. The 'unified' and 'without additional alignment' framing is therefore overstated.

The experimental support for the central SOTA claim is inconsistent. On UniAvatar-Bench, JoVA's gains over OVI are small (e.g., LSE-C 6.64 vs. 6.41, WER 0.18 vs. 0.23), and on Verse-Bench JoVA underperforms OVI on several metrics, including LSE-C (6.51 vs. 6.61), FD (1.10 vs. 0.97), CU (5.24 vs. 5.60), and PQ (5.61 vs. 6.20). The text also says 'OVI (6.41)' on Verse-Bench while Table 2 reports 6.61, indicating an unresolved inconsistency.

Comparisons with audio-driven methods are not fully apples-to-apples: audio-driven baselines receive ground-truth audio while JoVA generates audio, yet the paper directly compares lip-sync scores and claims to surpass them. No separate controlled experiment isolates the effect of generated audio quality on LSE-C.

Ablations are insufficient. The joint-attention vs. cross-attention comparison is only on UniAvatar-Bench, not Verse-Bench; the cross-attention with linear adaptation variant performs suspiciously poorly (LSE-C 1.63), suggesting implementation/tuning issues. No human evaluation, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported, despite small benchmark sizes (100 samples for UniAvatar-Bench).

Reproducibility is weak. The training corpus is collected from public sources, but no exact video list, filtering criteria, licensing/consent details, or data release statement is provided. Annotations depend on large pretrained models without human verification. Key implementation details are missing: text conditioning specifics, joint-attention mechanics, loss-weight schedule, classifier-free guidance details, compute requirements, and inference cost. Training a 12B×2 model for 130K steps is not practically reproducible for most labs.

The paper does not adequately analyze mouth-mask robustness: keypoint detector failures, occlusion, profile views, and temporal misalignment are not quantified. Appendix A provides only a qualitative zero-masking check, not a systematic validation of the mouth-region mask.

The writing and claims need correction. The abstract says 'Universe-Bench' while the experiments use 'Verse-Bench'; the conclusion claims SOTA despite mixed metrics; phrases like 'elegant' and 'state-of-the-art alignment' are not consistently supported. Limitations and broader societal risks (e.g., deepfake generation, identity misuse) are essentially absent beyond a brief research-use declaration.

Evaluation circularity is possible: WER is computed with Whisper-large-v3 on generated audio, while Whisper was also used to create transcripts during training. This could bias speech-generation metrics, and no independent ASR or human transcription check is provided.

No inference speed, memory, or training-cost comparison is given, despite the architectural-simplicity claim. Joint attention over concatenated video/audio/text tokens can be quadratic in total token length and may not be cheaper than carefully designed cross-attention, so the efficiency argument is unsubstantiated.

strengths: The paper proposes a clean, intuitive architectural idea: joint self-attention over video, audio, and text tokens in each transformer block, removing modality-specific fusion/cross-attention modules. This is conceptually simple and potentially more extensible than dual-branch fusion designs.

The mouth-area loss is simple yet highly effective. The ablation showing LSE-C rising from 1.39 to 6.64 when mouth-aware supervision is enabled provides strong empirical support for its importance in lip-speech synchronization.

The empirical results are strong overall. On UniAvatar-Bench, JoVA achieves the best or competitive scores across many metrics, including LSE-C, WER, audio quality, and video motion/aesthetic scores, and the 3.2B variant is notably competitive with much larger baselines.

The paper includes useful diagnostic studies: mouth-loss weight sensitivity, temporal-aligned RoPE, joint vs. cross-attention fusion, and model-scale comparison. These ablations largely support the claimed design choices.

The training-data construction and annotation pipeline is a valuable systems contribution: multi-source data, video/audio captions, and Whisper transcripts for speech supervision, enabling unified ambient-sound and human-speech generation.

The zero-masking validation in the appendix is a good sanity check for the mouth-region latent localization, increasing confidence that the mouth loss is applied to the intended spatial-temporal region.
weaknesses: There are several clarity and consistency issues. The paper alternates between 'Verse-Bench' and 'Universe-Bench', discusses 'Universe' vs. 'Universe-1', and the Verse-Bench text says JoVA 'slightly underperforms OVI (6.41)' while Table 2 reports OVI at 6.61 and JoVA at 6.51. Such inconsistencies weaken the presentation and make state-of-the-art claims harder to verify.

Some claims are overstated. On Verse-Bench, JoVA is not best on several key metrics: LSE-C is lower than OVI, FD is worse than OVI, and PQ is worse than OVI, yet the conclusion claims state-of-the-art alignment and overall generation fidelity. The paper should more carefully qualify 'outperforms' vs. 'competitive'.

Reproducibility is limited. Key implementation details are missing: token counts/sequence lengths, exact text-conditioning setup, attention masking, how separate modality branches interact with joint attention, training compute/hardware, CFG details, and evaluation sample selection. Code/weights/data are not clearly released.

The evaluation is restricted to two benchmarks, one of which (UniAvatar-Bench) is newly curated by the authors and not fully specified. Comparisons are mainly against OVI and Universe-1; several relevant recently cited unified audio-video methods (e.g., AV-DiT, JavisDiT, MM-Diffusion, Uniform, etc.) are not experimentally compared.

The mouth-aware loss relies on facial keypoint detection and assumes a detectable mouth region. The paper does not analyze robustness to profile views, occlusion, multiple faces, missing faces, or keypoint-detection failures, nor does it discuss possible training-data bias or privacy/consent concerns for talking-head video use.

The claim of 'no additional alignment modules' should be softened: temporal-aligned RoPE is a cross-modal synchronization prior, and keypoint-based mouth supervision is extra training-time supervision. These are not full fusion modules, but they are additional inductive biases/components.

The cross-attention ablation may be implementation-sensitive and possibly under-tuned; the conclusion that joint self-attention is 'essential' rests on two hand-designed cross-attention variants. A fairer parameter-matched and tuning-controlled comparison would strengthen the claim.

The paper lacks a limitations section and broader-impact discussion beyond a short declaration. For a human-centric video-audio generation model with speech capability, societal risks (misuse, deepfakes, identity/privacy) merit explicit discussion.

Some evaluation metrics may not fully capture joint audio-video generation quality, and it is unclear how LSE-C is computed on non-speech or non-face samples in Verse-Bench. The benchmark protocol needs more precise description.

strengths: Proposes a unified architecture that handles joint video-audio generation and editing in a single model, reducing reliance on task-specific fusion modules and fragmented pipelines.

The native joint self-attention over concatenated video, audio, and text tokens is simple and extensible, and the channel-wise conditioning strategy is a practical way to inject visual references without exploding token length.
The mouth-area loss is a simple but effective mechanism for improving lip-speech synchronization, and the ablation shows a clear benefit over the no-mouth-loss setting.
Constructs a large-scale multimodal corpus (~3M pairs) and introduces two evaluation benchmarks, with experiments on JoVABench-Gen, JoVABench-Edit, Verse-Bench, VBench, and human subjective studies.

Empirical results are broadly strong: JoVA achieves competitive or best results on many metrics, including lip-sync, audio quality, video fidelity, and motion, and the diagnostic studies support the architectural and loss choices.
The paper is generally well organized and clearly written, with helpful figures and tables, and it acknowledges several limitations of the current system.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core components build heavily on existing pretrained video/audio models, prior joint self-attention/MM-DiT designs, channel concatenation, and localized reconstruction losses; the contribution is largely a capable integration and data-construction effort rather than a fundamentally new algorithm.

The introduced JoVABench-Gen and JoVABench-Edit are central to the claims but are not described in sufficient detail: construction protocol, annotation process, sample diversity, filtering criteria, and potential bias are largely missing, making it difficult to assess their validity or independence from the proposed method.

Evaluation coverage is uneven. The main generation benchmark omits DeSync or a direct general-scene audio-video synchronization metric despite the metric being listed, while the editing benchmark omits generated audio quality and focuses on cascaded baselines using ground-truth audio, limiting conclusions about true joint audio-video editing.

The editing evaluation is narrow: training and evaluation emphasize human-speech scenes, and the paper acknowledges that general-scene audio-video editing remains unsupported. This weakens the broad 'joint video-audio editing' claim.

Several baselines are cascaded pipelines with ground-truth audio, which solve an easier task; although this is acknowledged, the lack of comparison to recent unified or audio-visual editing methods makes the state-of-the-art claim less convincing.

The abstract and conclusion overstate performance as state-of-the-art across benchmarks, but JoVA is not best on all metrics (e.g., WER, KL, ID in some tables), and the paper relies on 'best overall trade-off' rather than consistent superiority.

Reproducibility is limited: the system uses a 12B backbone, large-scale proprietary/curated data, and a data-synthesis pipeline with GPT-4o, FLUX, Wan2.2-Fun, Higgs-Audio, and lip-sync modules; neither the full dataset nor code appears to be released, and training details are insufficient for independent replication.
The synthetic editing data may inherit artifacts and biases from the foundation models used in its construction, and the paper does not analyze this distribution shift or its effect on evaluation.

The mouth-area loss depends on external facial keypoint detection and only applies to speech data; the architecture alone shows weak lip-sync without it, raising questions about generalization to non-speech, multi-speaker, or general audio-visual scenarios.
Minor presentation and consistency issues remain, such as missing metric entries, inconsistent use of DeSync, and occasional unclear or potentially erroneous table labels in the appendix.

strengths: Proposes a unified dual-branch architecture that handles joint video-audio generation and editing in a single model, reducing reliance on task-specific pipelines.
Uses channel-wise visual conditioning and audio token concatenation to incorporate reference images/videos/audio without excessive token expansion.
Introduces a simple mouth-area loss that is ablated and shown to substantially improve lip-sync metrics (LSE-C) on the proposed benchmark.

Constructs a large-scale training corpus of approximately 3M video-audio-text pairs and introduces JoVABench-Gen/JoVABench-Edit, with additional evaluations on Verse-Bench and VBench plus human subjective studies.
Provides broad quantitative comparisons across many metrics (audio quality, video fidelity, synchronization) and includes a limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The joint video-audio editing evaluation is not convincing: the baselines combine video editing with lip-sync models and use ground-truth audio, so they do not solve the same joint audio-video editing task, and the paper reports no audio editing quality or audio instruction-following metrics for JoVA. This makes the central editing claim unsupported.

The newly introduced JoVABench-Gen and JoVABench-Edit are author-constructed and evaluated by the authors, with insufficient details on construction, annotation protocol, difficulty, source distribution, filtering, and release plans. A 200-sample benchmark with no external validation is weak evidence for the claimed SOTA unified performance.

Comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: audio-driven models cannot generate audio but are included in joint-generation tables, missing metrics are omitted, and it is unclear how fairly prompts, inference settings, and reproduction protocols were controlled. No error bars, significance tests, or variance across runs are reported.

The technical novelty is overstated. Joint self-attention over concatenated multimodal tokens, channel-wise conditioning, and localized losses are all well-known components; the proposed design still relies on projectors and token/feature concatenation, so the claim of eliminating fusion modules is not fully accurate.

The architecture comparison and mouth-loss ablation are narrow and rely on a small set of metrics without variance. The very low LSE-C of one cross-attention variant (1.59) suggests possible implementation or tuning issues rather than a conclusive architectural finding.

Reproducibility is limited: the paper does not provide code, dataset release, or enough detail on keypoint detection, data filtering thresholds, synthetic editing prompt generation, or training of the 12B backbone. The 3M corpus includes proprietary/collected human-speech data without sufficient ethical/consent details.

The paper makes broad claims about unified editing and content creation while only demonstrating limited editing scenarios (primarily human-speech-centric) and acknowledging that general-scene audio-video editing data is unavailable. The evidence does not support the generality claimed in the abstract and introduction.

Evaluation metrics are not sufficient for joint multimodal quality. Lip-sync metrics are speech-only, DeSync is narrow, and many video/audio metrics are borrowed from separate traditions; no single rigorous protocol validates joint generation and editing simultaneously.

strengths: The paper presents a unified framework for joint video-audio generation and editing with a simple and extensible architecture. The use of native joint self-attention over video, audio, and text tokens removes complex task-specific cross-modal fusion modules and is well motivated.

The proposed channel-wise conditioning for visual reference avoids severe token expansion and naturally supports image/video reference conditioning, while the mouth-area loss provides a simple and effective way to improve lip-speech synchronization, as shown by a large LSE-C gain in the diagnostic study.

The work is supported by a large-scale data construction pipeline (~3M pairs) covering general scenes, human speech, and synthesized editing data, and it introduces two evaluation benchmarks (JoVABench-Gen and JoVABench-Edit) plus additional evaluation on Verse-Bench and VBench.

Empirical results are strong overall: JoVA achieves the best or highly competitive results across many generation, editing, and synchronization metrics, and the human subjective study further supports its perceptual quality and instruction-following ability.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and includes useful ablations on the mouth-loss weight and audio-video fusion strategies. The limitations are acknowledged honestly.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it largely builds on existing pretrained components (Waver, MMAudio VAE, temporal-aligned RoPE) and combines them with straightforward joint self-attention, channel conditioning, and a mouth-region loss. The algorithmic novelty over existing MM-DiT-style joint models is moderate.

Reproducibility is limited. The model is large (12B), training compute and hardware are not reported, and it is unclear whether the curated dataset, benchmarks, code, or model weights will be released. Several baselines are reproduced or borrowed from other papers, which weakens confidence in exact comparability.

The editing comparison is not against truly comparable joint video-audio editing systems; cascaded pipelines with ground-truth audio are used instead. Although this is acknowledged, the evaluation protocol is not fully apples-to-apples, and JoVA is not uniformly best on every reported metric (e.g., PC, CU, IB-TV, ID in some tables).

The introduced benchmarks contain only 200 samples each, and the paper does not provide sufficient details on benchmark annotation, instruction generation, human verification, or diversity. The claim of 'unified benchmarks' is therefore not fully substantiated from the main text.

The data construction pipeline depends heavily on closed or external foundation models (GPT-4o, FLUX, Wan2.2, Higgs-Audio, etc.), which may introduce teacher-model biases, artifacts, and licensing/reproducibility concerns. The paper does not analyze how such synthetic editing data affects evaluation or whether it overlaps with real-world distributions.

The mouth-area loss depends on accurate facial keypoint detection and may fail for non-frontal faces, occlusions, multiple people, or unusual poses; these failure modes are not analyzed. The added projector and mouth-region supervision also slightly complicate the claim that the method eliminates redundant alignment modules entirely.

The paper reports many automatic metrics but lacks error bars, statistical significance tests, and inference cost/throughput analysis. The VBench comparison borrows baseline numbers from other work, and it is not fully clear that all methods were evaluated under the same protocol.
